what: The sections of this article, each with a line and a paragraph, for showing what the reader has already read. Built by admin/build/summaries.py from admin/content/articles/summaries/.

sections.label: The opening
sections.line: RiskMandate and the ABP, for the person who decides
sections.para: A reader found the pages hard, saw the value in reporting what an agent can do, guessed it did not cover commercial agents or real time, and asked how it gets into the room. This answers all four: what it is, why it stays out of the agent's path, which agents it covers, and five ways in.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: It records what an agent can reach; others enforce
sections.para: For one agent in one deployment: the grant, the mandate, the gap and what stands in the way. It never sits in the agent's path, already has policies for commercial agents, measures the enterprise-assistant oversharing gap, extends to decision and workflow policies, and enters through questions already asked.

sections.label: The pages are hard to read
sections.line: The pages are precise, not clear; this is the short version
sections.para: The sites were written in the vocabulary the work needed: grant, mandate, delta, barrier, a 23-word grammar. That criticism is fair, and this article is the ten-minute version for someone deciding whether it matters.

sections.label: What it is, in one paragraph
sections.line: Grant, mandate, delta and barrier, for one agent
sections.para: An agent's credential lets it do far more than the job. The behaviour policy records what it can reach, what was authorised, the authority nobody accepted, and the barrier on each capability. Only a boundary enforced by something the grant does not include bounds anything; a prompt line does not, and how many controls are only prompt lines is measured per deployment.

sections.label: Yes, it reports what an agent can actually do
sections.line: It reports what an agent can actually do
sections.para: Thirteen prompts in the assistant you already use list its tools, draft what you wanted in three lists, and write the gap down; the list is longer than the tile that sold it. That is a self-report; paid levels measure the credential and a person signs the top one, though the pricing page marks its top two levels as specified, never run.

sections.label: Does it work with commercial agents?
sections.line: Policies for commercial agents, not integrations
sections.para: The library has policies for Claude with Gmail and Microsoft 365, ChatGPT, Claude Desktop, Google Workspace, Dropbox, n8n, Claude Code and GitHub Actions, from vendor pages or measurement. Connectors to a customer's systems are built per engagement, and none is a product yet. No Rovo, Copilot or Glean vault exists. Each barrier is marked as yours or the vendor's.

sections.label: The enterprise assistant that sees too much
sections.line: Rovo grants no new access; whose access depends on the identity
sections.para: Rovo honours existing permissions, with connector setup that varies by type. Risks: over-shared content becomes easy to find; the executing identity is the requester in chat, the connection account in automation, or the agent's own account, and an automation can read with one and publish to a wider audience; creation and use are open by default; a reported injection can send data out. Five checks test a real deployment.

sections.label: Is it real time?
sections.line: Not in the path, on purpose; runtimes enforce
sections.para: RiskMandate reads and models, with no enforcement point to slow or break an agent, which is why it can describe agents it cannot control. Enforcement belongs to gateways, hooks and runtimes: an ABP was compiled into Ruflo's rules and enforced live on an external adapter's memory operations, without changing Ruflo's running policy or other tools.

sections.label: Beyond what it can reach: who decides
sections.line: Beyond reach: who decides, on what evidence
sections.para: A behaviour policy answers may it, not is it right. Decision and workflow policies add who decides and in what order. The Northstar refund twin, a scripted simulation of thirteen synthetic cases with no model called, shows it in five minutes: a limit and good logs overpay $458 in a day; three policies get all thirteen right.

sections.label: How does it get into the room?
sections.line: Five questions already on somebody's desk
sections.para: Few people see how fast agents move, so nobody asks for an agent risk tool. The way in is a question with a deadline: a vendor contract, a customer's security questionnaire, an insurance renewal, the board's risk appetite where the UK Corporate Governance Code applies, or twenty minutes with your own assistant. None needs anyone to understand agents first.

sections.label: What I would like to hear back
sections.line: Tell us which question you are asked
sections.para: Readers in those rooms are asked which question they face and what answer would help. For an enterprise assistant like Rovo, the early access programme builds its behaviour policy for one real agent, in exchange for corrections.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: What is documented, simulated or not yet run
sections.para: No Rovo, Copilot or Glean vault exists, and Rovo's identities are from Atlassian's documentation, not a tenant test. RiskMandate does not enforce, and its top two levels have not been run. The injection report is historical and its current status unverified. The Northstar figures are a simulation, and self-reports are marked as weak evidence.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: riskmandate.ai, abp.sgit.ai, Atlassian's pages, and a review
sections.para: Both sites as read on 18 October 2026; Atlassian's Rovo privacy, trust, connector, identity, knowledge, automation safety, governance, MCP and tracker pages and its 6 October announcement; Microsoft's oversharing guidance; a third-party injection report; and a ChatGPT review, checked against them, that corrected the Rovo section.
